newsitem.title: USA: Blinder says Fed made right decision on rates.
newsitem.headline: Blinder says Fed made right decision on rates.

text.p: Alan Blinder, former vice chairman of the Federal Reserve, Thursday said the central bank acted appropriately this week when it opted not to raise interest rates.
"I think it was an extremely close call, and they did the right thing," Blinder told reporters after speaking at a Business Week symposium.
Blinder said the "preponderance of evidence" supported the idea that it would be best to wait.

He pointed out that data such as recent retail sales reports suggest that the economy is set to slow down in the closing months of this year, meaning that it might not be necessary for the Fed to tighten credit in order to rein in growth.
Blinder also discussed the long-term trends in the economy, saying he disagreed with those who say the economy is capable of growing at more than two to 2.5 percent without generating inflation.
Blinder noted that the economy has grown at only slightly more than two percent for the past few years, as both the unemployment rate and inflation have held steady.
If the true potential growth rate of the economy was a lot faster, unemployment would have fallen further by now, Blinder said.
He identified 5.6 percent as the likely level for the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment (NAIRU).
Blinder said 5.6 percent "seems to be an excellent estimate of the area in which inflation neither accelerates nor decelerates."

Although the jobless rate fell to 5.1 percent in August, Blinder said that if the economy slows the rate would likely move higher toward the range of 5.4 to 5.8 percent, which he said was a healthy area.
Blinder, asked whether Tuesday's decision by the Fed to keep rates steady was a sign officials were pursuing a policy of "opportunistic disinflation," which he has advocated, said he thought it was.

"More than anything else it was an expression of patience," he said of the decision. "If the Fed was hell-bent on getting to zero inflation as fast as possible it surely would have been raising interest rates the last few meetings."

He added, "The fact that (the Fed) has been patient ... is a very strong sign that the center of the Fed -- indeed a majority at the Fed -- believe in more opportunistic patience to bring the inflation down."

Under the opportunistic approach, policymakers do not actively attempt to push inflation down when it is already at low levels. Instead, they take advantage of naturally occuring economic downturns to lock in further gains against inflation. But if inflation seems set to pick up, policymakers following opportunisitic disinflation would strenously fight it.
